step.text:
Looking at the dimensions, the panel's 328px usable width with a tall viewport creates an aspect ratio that pushes the sky element below my minimum threshold of 150px, so the clamp constraint would activate. With those tighter dimensions, the bird scales down to 42px and the runway fits in about 89 units, giving a traversal time under a second at the animation speed.

I'm weighing a few approaches: either accept the tight reaction time as an edge case, add letterboxing with the field color, or adjust the bird's horizontal position proportionally as the sky narrows to preserve runway distance. The cleanest solution seems to be letting the bird move inward as the sky gets narrower rather than clamping the sky width itself, which keeps the runway consistent without visual padding.

Actually, I can simplify this entirely by dropping the clamp altogether—the panel has a hard floor at 360 anyway, so there's no risk of it collapsing to nothing. The game will just be slightly harder at narrow widths and easier at wide ones, which is honest and matches how other side-scrollers behave across viewports. Now I need to check whether keeping the bird at 0.32 of the sky width maintains a reasonable runway, or if I should scale that fraction to keep the runway more constant across different panel sizes.

step.text:
I'm working through the layout dimensions for the game field. With a default width of 480 pixels minus padding, the field is about 448 wide, and based on the screenshot proportions, roughly 950 pixels tall, giving me an aspect ratio around 0.47. This breaks down to about 170 pixels for the sky, 54 for the bird position, and 116 for the runway, which works out to a reasonable 1.2 second flight time. At the narrowest viewport of 360 pixels, the proportions scale down to 328 wide with adjusted sky and runway heights, bringing the flight time down to about 0.88 seconds.

The challenge is that at narrow widths, the bird needs enough runway ahead to make the game playable—roughly 115 units at the current speed to maintain that 1.2 second window. But a tall narrow panel doesn't show much sky ahead, so I'm considering anchoring the sky width at a fixed 240 pixels instead and letting the height float based on the aspect ratio. This would give me a taller sky in portrait orientations, making the flap mechanic feel more proportional to the screen and spreading the pipe gaps over a larger vertical range.

The tradeoff is that anchoring height keeps the game feel consistent across all panel sizes—the bird's flap height, gap size, and bird scale all stay the same relative to the screen—while anchoring width would make narrow panels require more flapping to cross the same visual distance. I think keeping the feel consistent matters more than reaction time varying slightly, so I'm leaning toward sticking with the height anchor and accepting that narrow panels are tighter. But 0.88 seconds of runway at the narrowest is pretty rough, so I'm exploring a compromise: capping how far right the bird can spawn in wider panels to prevent them from becoming trivially easy, while ensuring narrow panels always have a minimum runway.

Actually, I'm overthinking this. The honest framing is that the sky is as wide as the field and the bird stands 30% in from the left. A 360px panel is the narrowest anyone can make it, and yes, the game gets harder there—just like any side-scroller is harder on a narrow screen. Real Flappy Bird on a phone gives about 1.2 seconds of runway, and we're hitting 0.9 seconds at the extreme and 1.2 seconds at the default, which is fine.

Wait, there's a cleaner approach I keep skirting around: what if pipe spacing and speed are both defined in world units, and the world itself...

Actually, no. I need to stop and ship the simple rule. The sky width scales with the aspect ratio, the bird sits at 30% of the width, no clamping. But there's one edge case I should guard against: if the field ever becomes 1 pixel wide, the sky collapses to nearly zero and pipes spawn at 40 while the bird is at 0, which means instant death. The panel has a minimum of 360 pixels though, and the field is measured properly, so a zero-size field should fall back to the default sky width via the height check.

When the panel closes with a CSS transition, the outer div shrinks but the inner content stays fixed and gets clipped—the game field doesn't actually resize, so that's safe. And switching tabs unmounts the whole GameView anyway. Still, a minimum floor on the sky width is cheap protection against any weird measurement edge cases, so I'll keep that in place.

I'll set NARROWEST to 120—at the narrowest real panel width of 328, the sky calculates to 124, so the floor never actually triggers in practice. If it somehow did engage on a degenerate case, the image would just clip at the right edge, which is fine. No letterboxing needed.

Updating flappy.ts now with NARROWEST set to 120 and birdX adjusted to 0.3...

Now I'm working through the FlappyGame component—it needs to hold onto the box reference, expand the game canvas when the window resizes, and trigger repaints whenever the box changes. I'm running into a timing issue with the effects though: Field's effect fires after its child FlappyGame's effects, but FlappyGame is actually the parent rendering Field, so the effect ordering gets a bit tangled here.

I'm setting up the state to track the box dimensions and computing the sky width from those dimensions, then using effects to widen the game and repaint the canvas. There's a careful optimization where `widen` returns the same object if nothing changed, so React won't trigger unnecessary updates. On mount, the box starts at zero but the sky width calculation has a guard that defaults to 240, which matches what `newFlappy()` uses initially, so everything stays consistent until the real box dimensions arrive. When `start()` gets called, it should use the current sky value, so I need to make sure that's available in the dependency array.

Now I'm moving on to TetrisGame and just swapping out the width state for the box state, then I'll write out both components.

Looking at the images more carefully now—in image b, the first disc has that mesh pattern in blue and purple, while the second disc coming in is a dark maroon color, followed by the vertical line on the right. Image a shows the first disc in a grey-lavender tone with the vertical line positioned similarly. The vertical line appears taller than the disc itself. Measuring across the scaled images, the line comes out to roughly 1.22 times the disc diameter, which aligns pretty closely with the SVG box height ratio of about 1.15—the slight difference could be antialiasing blur on the line's edges. Positioning the line horizontally, it sits about 261 pixels to the right of the first disc's center in the original coordinates.

Converting to user units using the scale factor, that puts the line at x=644, which lands right at or just inside the SVG viewport's right edge at x=652. The faint white or grey coloring at that edge is a telltale sign of an edge-clamp artifact.

The mask region actually extends much further right to x=812, but Chromium clips the rendered layer to the viewport boundary at 652—exactly where the line appears. When masked content gets drawn into a transparency layer and sampled at that boundary, you get artifacts from the compositing process trying to sample just outside the clipped region.

The solution is simple: keep the painted rectangles (the sky, flash, and color rects) from extending all the way to the viewport edge. Instead of letting them reach x=812 and getting hard-clipped at 652, I should constrain them to stay within the visible bounds.

Looking at the disc animations more carefully, the rightmost disc starts at scale 0.32 with a translate of 64px, putting it around x=566 at the beginning. Even accounting for the overshoot scaling up to 1.09 at the 55% mark, the maximum extent is around 643.7—still under the 652 viewport edge. So the current 180-pixel bleed is actually excessive for what's needed.

The real issue is that the mask and paint shouldn't share an edge with the clip boundary. The SVG viewport itself acts as the clipping mechanism (via its default overflow behavior), so I need to ensure there's enough breathing room between the visible content and that viewport edge, or reconsider how the clipping is being applied. The issue is the mask bitmap's edge clamping — when Skia samples the mask at the clip boundary, it's pulling from the mask's last column which should be black, but something about how the mask is rasterized or stored is causing that edge to leak through. Rather than dig deeper into the exact mechanism, I should just fix it empirically.

Let me reproduce this with the probe harness first — that's the fastest way to confirm the fix. The user's already reported it twice, so I need to stop guessing and get concrete data.

Actually, wait. Let me reconsider something simpler: `crew-flash` is a white rectangle covering the whole field with a mask applied, and `crew-sweep` is an ellipse that translates 880 units with `transform-box: view-box`. Both fade out on specific timelines — the flash ends around 610ms, the sweep around 760ms, and the discs around 720ms. The line disappearing near the end matches these timings perfectly. Looking at the images, the line is visible in the early frames when only the first disc has arrived, and it's also there in the later images.

In the first image, the disc is fully sized and greyish-lavender, which suggests the mesh transition is still ramping up around 100-150ms. At that point, the sweep animation has just started at the left side (cx=-96), so the line exists well before the sweep reaches the right edge. I need to figure out what's actually at the right edge from the beginning.

Looking at the second image, there's a visible dark maroon disc at position 2 (cx=316) that's partially arrived, but the rightmost disc slot at 502 is empty. The vertical line at around 644 units isn't a disc at all—it must be something else, maybe the paint layer's right edge leaking through the SVG viewport clip. At rest, the mesh, flash, and sweep all render with opacity 0 due to their `both` fill states, so they shouldn't be visible, yet the line appears during the animation.

The key difference is that when the disc groups animate, Chromium promotes the SVG to a composited layer and re-rasterizes it differently—possibly due to will-change or transform animations. This per-frame re-rasterization of the mask bitmap at a coarser scale could introduce edge artifacts. The line at x=812 might actually be the mask region boundary being rasterized at a different scale, though that would place it 160 units past the viewport edge, which seems too far off-screen.

Let me recalculate the coordinate conversions: if the line is at 812 units, that's about 47 CSS pixels from the disc center, which would translate to around 1311 in the b-big scale—but the measured line is at 1055. Working backward from 652 units gives 36 CSS pixels, or 1067 in b-big, which matches the measurement of 1055 much more closely.

I've pinpointed the issue: the line sits exactly at the SVG viewport's right edge at x=652, spanning the full height. It's a clipping artifact from the masked, over-painted layer—Chromium is leaving a hairline of unmasked or clamped content at the clip boundary while the mask rasterizes each frame. The solution is to shrink the painted rectangles and mask region inward from the viewport edge so there's transparent space between the paint and the clip boundary, eliminating the leak.

The challenge is that the sweep extends to x=880 and the mesh must cover the discs, which occupy x ∈ [0, 644] and y ∈ [0, 260]. Since the viewBox spans [-20, 652] × [-20, 280], I can inset the paint field to something like [-8, 640] × [-8, 268], creating a 12-unit buffer before the clip edge at 652. The mask's black rectangle only needs to cover wherever the paint exists, and since the paint only shows through the white disc regions, I just need to ensure the paint bounds encompass the discs' actual extent accounting for the scale factor.

With the paint field at [-12, 644] × [-12, 272], that leaves roughly 8 units of gutter on each side—about 0.55 CSS pixels, which is tight but workable at standard DPI. To get more breathing room, I could increase the ROOM constant from 20 to 40, which expands the overall stage height and element size, but the height style property scales proportionally to keep the disc size at 18px, so the visual appearance stays consistent while gaining more gutter space.

Alternatively, I could set overflow to visible on the SVG so nothing clips at the viewport boundary, letting the paint rects extend freely—though they'd still be masked by the disc shapes anyway.  The real question is whether the clipping is actually necessary: the mask itself should prevent content from showing outside the discs, so maybe the clip is there to handle antialiasing artifacts at the mask edges, or perhaps there was an issue with the flash painting beyond the intended bounds that clipping solved.

The cleanest approach would be to align the mask region and the painted rectangles to the same dimensions, then add a proper gutter around them so nothing sits right at the boundary—that way the only visible edges are the discs themselves, and we avoid any artifacts from coinciding paint and mask edges.

But wait, if the mask region and paint rect are identical, their edges would still create that hard boundary. The real issue is at the clip edge itself—when Skia renders the mask and content to offscreen buffers, both sized to the intersection of bounds and clip, the last pixel column at the clip boundary gets partially covered, and that's where the sampling error leaks through.

Let me check if the mask is being rasterized at a different device scale. The mask region is 992×620 user units, and at the element's scale (0.1386 px/unit at 2x), that's about 137×86 device pixels—no downscaling there. Or maybe the artifact is actually coming from the mesh's blob gradients bleeding through the crew-blob transforms instead. I need to stop speculating and actually reproduce this.

I'll build a minimal test case to capture frames at 2x device scale and see what's happening. I don't even need the full Tailwind build—just the mark with currentColor for the text and the CSS animation.

The cleanest approach is to use Vite with the real CrewMark component since it's standalone and only imports crew-mark.ts. I'll wrap it in a div with the data-lit attribute to avoid loading audio, then extract just the `.crew-*` CSS rules from styles.css into the probe rather than running the whole Tailwind pipeline.

Actually, I can leverage the Tailwind Vite plugin that's already in the repo — it handles the `@import "tailwindcss"` line properly. I'll place the probe under node_modules/.markprobe and follow the pattern from cover-sheet.mjs to set this up.
